In order to publish obituaries a name and phone number of funeral home/cremation society is required. If the body of the deceased has been donated to the University of Minnesota Anatomy Bequest Program, or a similar program, their phone number is required for verification.
Please allow enough time to contact them especially during their limited weekend hours.
A death certificate is also acceptable for this purpose but only one of these two options are necessary.

We are not allowed to reference other media sources with a guestbook or an obituary placed elsewhere when placing an obituary in print and online. We may place a website for a funeral home or a family email for contact instead; contact us with any questions regarding this matter.

Online:
Changes to an online obituary can be handled through the obituary desk. Call us with further questions.

 By Edward Lotterman PUBLISHED: October 25, 2026 at 9:01 AM CDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Edward Lotterman 
 We have just had the annual ritual announcement of the percentage by which Social Security payments will be increased for 2027. The same boost also applies to Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, plus VA disability compensation plus both military and federal civil service retirees.
 It makes a big difference to the 76 million enrolled in programs administered by the Social Security Administration and others.
 Silly online personal finance publications tout “a big increase.” The average recipient, however, is more likely to grumble about meagerness than celebrate new wealth. Hardly anyone questions whether this 54-year-old automatic annual adjustment really is economically efficient and fair or whether it should be overhauled.
 Start with the complaints. The first comes from simple misunderstandings. One is that the cost of living adjustment isn’t based on a full year, it just considers three months. This shouldn’t make sense but is a belief that one encounters often.
 Fact is, the adjustment certainly is based on 12 months of price changes. But rather than being a December Consumer Price Index to prior-year December CPI comparison, it involves third quarters. This year compares the third quarter of 2026 to third quarter 2025. So it is the average of the CPI numbers for July, August and September 2026 over the average of those for the same three months in 2025.
 Why the rigmarole? First, the Social Security Administration needs to know the increase before the end of the year to calculate all the new amounts. Beneficiaries get deposits in their bank accounts in three batches on the second, third and fourth Wednesdays of the month. But the Bureau of Labor Statistics that tabulates most price indexes needs time to compile the CPI for the month just ended and release it between the 10th and 14th. So the CPI for December at the end of 2026 would not be available before the first 2027 payments already had to go out.
 The SSA could instead compare a single month like September or October to the same month 12 months earlier. Unfortunately, price indexes bounce around on a month-to month basis. If September 2026 happened to be a month with a spike and September 2025 had been flat, the computed COLA for 2027 would be too large compared to the true 12-month rise calculated after year-end. And if 2026 had the flat September and the upward blip had been in September 2025, the resulting COLA would be too small.
 Got that? If not, here is more detail on indexes in general. The press often confuses the public in their reporting of monthly changes in price indexes. The CPI is cited as a percentage change. That isn’t true. The CPI itself has no units, not dollars and not percentages. It is just a numerical scale set at 100 at a time when prices of a given “market basket” of thousands of goods and services are recorded. For many years, that starting point was prices in 1967. A single-year starting point is common for all sorts of other specialized price indexes. But for some reason, an updating in the mid-1980s changed the CPI’s base “year” to the average of prices over three years, 1982-1984.
 Thus when the CPI for “all urban wage earners and clerical workers,” the one used for COLAS, was reported last week as 330.654, it means that prices in September were 3.30654 times as high as they averaged over 1982 through 1984. That is the number for a single month. But the COLA comes from the three-month July-September quarter. That average of the index for that is 328.746.
 Now go back to 2025. Its average of the same third-quarter months was 317.265. Divide the 2026 average by the 2025 one and you get an increase by a factor of 1.03619. Change that to a percentage increase and round to one decimal point. Thus, prices in third-quarter 2026 were 3.6% higher than they were in third quarter 2025. Hence payments in 2027 will be 3.6% higher than this year.
 No, a third-quarter over third-quarter increase won’t be exactly the same as the December over December increases for the same year, but will be very close and will average out over time. The differences will be slightly up as often as slightly down. Whether computed at year end or in some given quarter, COLAS over 5, 10, or any other amount of years will match overall CPI increases in the same period.
 Frequent complaint 2. There are several different consumer price indexes. These vary with the prices of particular sets of goods and services for different groups of people that end up being tabulated. The two most common are the CPI for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) covering 90% of the population, and the narrower CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which covers approximately 30% of the population. (Search “BLS Consumer Price Indexes Overview” for a portal into tons of information on U.S price indexes.)
 It is the second, CPI-W, that is used to determine annual COLAS. This gives rise to many conspiracy theories that one somehow disadvantages the public if used rather than the other. But these beliefs are unfounded. Using the CPI-W, a $1,000 monthly benefit in 2000 would have grown to $1,869.56 for 2026. Using the CPI-U it would be $1,871.05.
 A second criticism is more valid. Retired people have a different pattern of purchases than does the general population. There thus should be a special CPI covering a “market basket” of goods and services for the elderly that would be a more fair metric for retiree COLAs. A special CPI for the elderly might give higher increases.
 This one actually exists — the R-CPI-E, or Research Consumer Price Index for the Elderly. “Research” here means that it is still being validated by statisticians and has smaller sample sizes and less fine resolution than established indexes. Over the same quarter century span, use of this index would have increased a $1,000 payment in 2000 to $1,917.21 for 2026. That $46 a month above the two general indexes cited would have made a difference to many people. Congress could make this change in a very simple bill, but the houses are so dysfunctional that not even this is possible.
 Unfortunately, such details that prompt squabbles in the short run pale in comparison to huge long-run issues no one talks about. Is it really sound that payments going to 76 million people today, and that will go to virtually everyone in the long run, really hang to a great degree on almost farcical events more than half-century ago? Is it really credible that a single starting number established in 1972 that was then compounded forward 54 times by an imperfect indicator is necessarily either just or economically efficient today?
 Congress deliberated on fair and sustainable payments nine times in the 32 years between first benefits checks issued in 1940 and their current indexation in 1972. Why has Congress not reviewed the COLA system? Why had it not revisited any aspect of Social Security since the Greenspan Commission recommendations of 1984?
 Answering that takes one back to a half-century to the career of a powerful congressman and his alcohol-befogged relationship with a D.C. stripper who styled herself as Fanne Foxe, the Argentine Firecracker.
 Here’s the story:
 During GOP President Richard Nixon’s first term, 1968 to 1972, Wilbur Mills, a powerful Democratic congressman from Arkansas, implemented plans to become president. A high achiever, he had first been elected to Congress at age 30 in 1938. He rose rapidly and by 1972 had headed the House Ways and Means Committee for 14 years. Thus controlling all tax legislation and many key spending categories, including Social Security, Rep. Mills was perhaps the most powerful member of Congress.
 Mills started plan to become president early. In 1969, with the CPI up 4.7%, a newly inaugurated Nixon called for a 7% increase in Social Security benefits. Mills pushed through 15%, which the spending-conscious Nixon signed reluctantly. The next year, after a 6.2% CPI jump, Nixon’s budget included a 6% benefits boost. Mills countered with 10% and carried the day.
 Inflation rates eased in 1972, but the rising cost of living remained a major issue for voters in an election year. Nixon had two proposals, a 5% increase plus a new automatic COLA, or cost of living adjustment, every year going forward. Mills glommed onto the COLA idea, but outbid Nixon with a 20% overall increase first. Nixon opposed this but eventually acquiesced in the face of wide public support and an adamant Congress. And, foreshadowing Donald Trump, Nixon was able to get a statement printed on every new monthly check that the increase had been signed into law by he, Nixon, himself.
 Mills stood victorious on the policy field. He ended up not running in 1972, but thought himself well-positioned with voters for 1976. And he planned to keep pushing large Social Security benefit increases as a core strategy.
 Unfortunately, Mills ruined his chances with a chaotic private life. Time magazine had described him as “one of the most disciplined, straight-laced, and intensely focused lawmakers” in Washington. He was not known as a womanizer. However, despite being a devout Methodist, his steadily growing addiction to alcohol led him into a 17-month affair with the stripper, “Fanne Foxe, The Argentine Firecracker,” 27 years his junior.
 Things fell apart. There were two interactions between the lovers that ended up with police intervention. The second time Fanne had two black eyes when pulled sputtering from the Washington, D.C, Tidal Basin just south of the Jefferson Memorial. At the end of his term a disgraced Mills retired to Arkansas for treatment and then several years establishing alcohol treatment efforts in his home state. His former lover went back on stage as Fanne Foxe, The Tidal Basin Bombshell.
 It is easy to laugh, but while exploiting benefit increases for crass political ends, Mills did understand Social Security backwards and forwards in a way that no member of Congress in the last 20 years has ever mastered. And was willing to act on it.

 The program still could become more fiscally sustainable, more efficient and more just. But that requires knowledge and integrity at both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue — characteristics notably lacking in our current time.
 St. Paul economist and writer Edward Lotterman can be reached at stpaul@edlotterman.com .
